explanation: There are 650 Members of Parliament in the House of Commons, each elected to represent one constituency.

angles.q: How many constituencies is the UK divided into?
How many MPs does each constituency elect?

explanation: The Scottish Parliament has 129 Members of the Scottish Parliament, known as MSPs.

angles.q: Members of the Scottish Parliament are known by which abbreviation?

explanation: The Scottish Parliament sits at Holyrood in Edinburgh.

angles.q: The Scottish Parliament building is known by which name?

explanation: The Northern Ireland Assembly meets at Stormont in Belfast.

angles.q: The Northern Ireland Assembly building is known by which name?

explanation: Serious criminal offences in England, Wales and Northern Ireland are tried in the Crown Court before a judge and a jury of 12.

angles.q: Which court in England and Wales hears the most serious criminal cases?
How many jurors sit in a Crown Court trial?

explanation: Minor criminal offences in England, Wales and Northern Ireland are dealt with in Magistrates' Courts by magistrates, who are unpaid members of the local community.

angles.q: Which court deals with minor criminal offences in England and Wales?
Are magistrates paid for their work?
wrong: Yes, they receive a full salary
Yes, they are paid per case

explanation: Scotland has its own legal system. Minor offences are heard in Justice of the Peace Courts, and serious ones in the Sheriff Court or High Court.

angles.q: Which court hears minor criminal cases in Scotland?
angles.a: The Justice of the Peace Court

angles.q: How many people sit on a Scottish jury?

explanation: A general election must be held at least every five years, and MPs are elected by the first past the post system.

angles.q: Under first past the post, which candidate becomes the MP?
angles.a: The one with the most votes in the constituency
wrong: The one with more than half of all votes cast
The one chosen by the party leader
The one with the most national support

explanation: You can vote in a UK general election at 18, provided you are on the electoral register and eligible.

angles.q: You must be on which list in order to vote?

explanation: The Prime Minister lives at 10 Downing Street and also has a country house called Chequers.

angles.q: What is the name of the Prime Minister's country house?

explanation: The Speaker chairs debates in the House of Commons, keeps order, and must be politically neutral.

angles.q: Does the Speaker of the House of Commons remain an MP?
angles.a: Yes, they still represent their constituency
wrong: No, they give up their seat
No, they join the House of Lords

explanation: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of countries, most of which were once part of the British Empire. It has no power over its members.

angles.q: What power does the Commonwealth have over its member states?
wrong: It can declare war on behalf of members

explanation: The UK is one of five permanent members of the UN Security Council, which works to resolve international disputes.

angles.q: How many permanent members does the UN Security Council have?

explanation: The NHS provides healthcare for everyone normally resident in the UK, and most treatment is free at the point of use.

angles.q: To register with a doctor, you normally contact what?

explanation: Income tax is paid on earnings, and most employees have it deducted automatically through the PAYE system.

angles.q: What does PAYE stand for?

explanation: You must be at least 17 to drive a car in the UK, and vehicles over three years old need an annual MOT test.

angles.q: At what age can vehicles first require an annual MOT test?

section: The values and principles of the UK
explanation: The fundamental principles of British life are democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs, and participation in community life.

angles.q: Which of these is one of the fundamental principles of British life?
angles.a: Tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs
wrong: Loyalty to a single political party

angles.q: Which of these is one of the fundamental principles of British life?

section: The values and principles of the UK
explanation: Residents are expected to respect and obey the law, respect the rights of others, treat others with fairness, look after themselves and their family, and look after the area they live in and the environment.

angles.q: Which of these is a responsibility of everyone living in the UK?
angles.a: Looking after the area you live in and the environment

angles.q: Which of these is a responsibility of everyone living in the UK?
wrong: Working in a public service job

section: The values and principles of the UK
explanation: Rights shared by everyone in the UK include freedom of belief and religion, freedom of speech, freedom from unfair discrimination, a right to a fair trial, and a right to join in the election of a government.

angles.q: Which of these is a right shared by everyone resident in the UK?

explanation: At a citizenship ceremony, new citizens make an oath or affirmation of allegiance to the monarch and a pledge to respect the rights, freedoms and laws of the UK.

angles.q: What do new citizens receive at the end of a citizenship ceremony?

explanation: The UK is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Great Britain refers only to England, Scotland and Wales.

angles.q: Which country is part of the UK but not part of Great Britain?
What do the letters UK stand for?
angles.a: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
wrong: The United Kingdom of England and Wales
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

explanation: The capital of the UK is London. Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland, Cardiff of Wales and Belfast of Northern Ireland.

angles.q: What is the capital city of Scotland?
Of which country is Cardiff the capital?

explanation: The currency of the UK is the pound sterling, with the symbol £. There are 100 pence in a pound.

angles.q: How many pence are there in a pound?
What symbol is used for the pound sterling?

explanation: The Union Flag, often called the Union Jack, combines the crosses of St George, St Andrew and St Patrick. Wales is not represented.

angles.q: By what other name is the Union Flag commonly known?

explanation: The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man are Crown dependencies. They are not part of the UK and have their own governments.

angles.q: Are the Channel Islands part of the UK?
wrong: Yes, they are part of England
Yes, they are a fifth country of the UK
No, they are part of France
